\section[l'acompte]{l'acompte — the down payment, the part payment}

\label{lesson:FR-C433-acompte}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the cleaning, then the French for faulty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'acompte}
\textbf{l'acompte} — \textquotedblleft{}the down payment, the part payment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Pour le gîte, nous avons versé un acompte de cent euros.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{For the cottage we paid a hundred euros up front.}
\end{quote}

A masculine noun. \emph{Verser un acompte} — to pay a part in advance.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acompte} comes from \emph{à compte} 'on account', from \emph{compte}, built on \emph{compter} 'to count', which goes back to Latin \emph{computāre} (Lewis \& Short). EtymDB does not list it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'acompte}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'acompte}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{l'acompte}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for the cleaning, then the French for faulty, then say \emph{l'acompte} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does l'acompte mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The down payment, the part payment\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[les arrhes]{les arrhes — the deposit (that is not refunded)}

\label{lesson:FR-C433-arrhes}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for faulty, then the French for the down payment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: les arrhes}
\textbf{les arrhes} — \textquotedblleft{}the deposit (that is not refunded)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Si vous annulez, vous perdez les arrhes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If you cancel, you lose the deposit.}
\end{quote}

Feminine plural: \emph{des arrhes}. The \emph{h} is silent.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{arrhes} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{arrha} 'pledge' (EtymDB), which came from Greek \emph{arrhab\'{\={o}}n}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{les arrhes}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{les arrhes}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for faulty, then the French for the down payment, then say \emph{les arrhes} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[dédommager]{dédommager — to compensate}

\label{lesson:FR-C433-dedommager}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the down payment, then the French for the deposit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dédommager}
\textbf{dédommager} — \textquotedblleft{}to compensate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La compagnie a dédommagé les passagers du vol annulé.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The airline compensated the passengers of the cancelled flight.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Dédommager quelqu'un de quelque chose}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dédommager} is built from \emph{dé-} 'un-' and \emph{dommage} 'harm', which goes back to Latin \emph{damnum} 'loss' (Lewis \& Short); EtymDB lists the verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dédommager}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dédommager}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{dédommager}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for the down payment, then the French for the deposit, then say \emph{dédommager} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does dédommager mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To compensate\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[le dédommagement]{le dédommagement — the compensation}

\label{lesson:FR-C433-dedommagement}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the deposit, then the French for to compensate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: le dédommagement}
\textbf{le dédommagement} — \textquotedblleft{}the compensation\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
L'hôtel nous a offert un repas en dédommagement.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The hotel offered us a meal by way of compensation.}
\end{quote}

\emph{En dédommagement} — as compensation.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dédommagement} is built on \emph{dédommager} with \emph{-ment} (EtymDB). \emph{Dédommager} comes from \emph{dommage} 'harm', from Latin \emph{damnum} 'loss' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[indemniser]{indemniser — to pay damages to, to indemnify}

\label{lesson:FR-C433-indemniser}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for to compensate, then the French for the compensation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: indemniser}
\textbf{indemniser} — \textquotedblleft{}to pay damages to, to indemnify\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
L'assurance va nous indemniser pour la valise perdue.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The insurance is going to pay us for the lost suitcase.}
\end{quote}

Formal, used by insurers: \emph{l'indemnisation}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{indemniser} is built on \emph{indemne} 'unharmed', a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{indemnis}, from \emph{in-} 'not' and \emph{damnum} 'loss' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
